259304461_eee883ba.text: The locus coeruleus (LC) is a collection of neurons, located bilaterally within the dorsal pons, adjacent to the fourth ventricle (Dahlstroem et al., 1964). LC neurons are distinguished from surrounding structures by their production of the neurotransmitter noradrenaline (NA), which in turn facilitates the brain-wide modulatory role of this nucleus (Berridge & Waterhouse, 2003). By projecting to almost the entire brain, the LC-NA system modulates ongoing brain activity, thereby influencing some of the most salient brain functions, including cognition (Usher et al., 1999), memory (Sara, 2015), arousal (Carter et al., 2010)), mood (McCall et al., 2015) and the central limb of the stress response (Valentino et al., 2008). In addition, the LC also modulates the physiology of various peripheral systems including the control of respiration (Carvalho et al., 2014)(Gargaglioni et al., 2010) and cardiac function (Biancardi et al., 2014)(Patrone et al., 2014)(Yao et al., 2005)

259304461_f7fa6d4a.text: .Central to LC function, in both health and disease, is the spontaneous firing rate (FR) of the principal neurons which determine the pattern and amount of NA release

259304461_29da31f0.text: .In the awake state and in in vitro preparations, LC neurons characteristically fire action potentials spontaneously, with a frequency ranging from ~1 to 5 Hz (Berridge & Waterhouse, 2003)
